page: Microsoft Azure D48as_v4 is a general-purpose virtual machine belonging to the DASv4 series. Powered by the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor, it runs on a dedicated 24-core, 48-thread AMD EPYC 7763 processor clocked at up to 3.525 GHz on the x86_64 architecture. The system provides 192.0 GB of system memory, matching the standard general-purpose ratio of 4.0 GB per vCPU. Hardware features include AVX, AES, VAES, and SHA cryptographic extensions, alongside 32 MB of L3 cache. It also integrates 412 GB of temporary local SSD storage, though it does not contain dedicated hardware GPU accelerators.

Benchmark results demonstrate strong parallel computing capabilities, with top-quartile results in stress-ng multi-core testing, PassMark CPU evaluation, and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression. Single-core performance falls in the upper quartile for stress-ng and shows average throughput in Geekbench execution. Memory throughput is solid, recording top-decile metrics in PassMark memory testing, while maintaining standard bandwidth scores across large-block sequential read and write operations.

The 1:4 vCPU-to-memory configuration and high core count offer a balanced resource profile for multi-threaded applications. The absence of hardware acceleration makes large-scale model inference inefficient, as seen in lower-quartile tokens-per-second scores for 70B parameter models, but lightweight text generation remains viable. The instance is well-suited for distributed compilation tasks, mid-sized relational database engines, enterprise application tiers, and multi-threaded ETL pipelines that leverage local temporary SSD storage for caching.
description: Microsoft Azure D48as_v4 is a general-purpose virtual machine equipped with 48 dedicated vCPUs derived from a 24-core AMD EPYC 7763 processor operating at up to 3.525 GHz. It provides 192.0 GB of RAM alongside 412 GB of bundled local SSD storage, maintaining a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio. Compute benchmarks show strong multi-core performance in stress-ng, Geekbench, and PassMark tests, supported by top-tier PassMark memory subsystem throughput. The platform lacks discrete GPU acceleration, rendering it ill-suited for large-scale machine learning workloads, where token generation rates decline significantly. However, its balanced allocation of high-density processing power, solid memory bandwidth, and integrated temporary storage makes it an efficient option for enterprise application hosting, batch ETL jobs, multi-threaded software builds, and relational database deployments requiring consistent CPU allocation.
